7
An object is projected horizontally. The object falls a vertical distance y and travels a horizontal
distance x before landing on the ground.
direction of
projection
vertical

landing
point
horizontal
distance
A second object is projected horizontally with the same initial velocity and falls a vertical distance
4y before landing on the ground.
Assume that air resistance is negligible.
Which horizontal distance does the second object travel?
A
x
B
2x
C
4x
D
16x

hints: Notice the projection is horizontal, so initial vertical velocity is zero and the time to reach the landing point is set only by the vertical distance $y$ and $g$.
Use $y = \frac{1}{2}gt^2$ for the vertical fall, so flight time $t$ is proportional to $\sqrt{y}$ - work out how $t$ changes when $y$ becomes $4y$.
Horizontally there is no acceleration, so use $x = ut$ with the same $u$ for both objects - multiply that unchanged $u$ by your new flight time to compare the ranges.
walkthrough: Treat horizontal and vertical motions separately. Horizontally velocity $u$ is constant because air resistance is negligible. Vertically initial velocity is zero and acceleration is $g$.
For the first object, vertical motion gives $y = \frac{1}{2}gt_1^2$, so $t_1 = \sqrt{2y/g}$. Its horizontal range is $x = ut_1$.
For the second object, vertical distance is $4y$, so $4y = \frac{1}{2}gt_2^2$ and $t_2 = \sqrt{2(4y)/g} = \sqrt{4}\sqrt{2y/g}$.
Hence $t_2 = 2t_1$. The flight time doubles, not quadruples, because of the $t^2$ in the vertical equation.
With the same $u$, the new range is $ut_2 = u(2t_1) = 2x$. This is option B.

A.explanation: Time in the air increases when the vertical drop increases, so with the same horizontal velocity the range cannot stay as $x$.

B.explanation: Fall time doubles for $4y$ because $t = \sqrt{2y/g}$, and with the same $u$ the range $x = ut$ also doubles to $2x$.

C.explanation: This assumes horizontal distance is directly proportional to vertical distance, but $y$ depends on $t^2$ so time only increases as $\sqrt{y}$.

D.explanation: This squares the factor of 4, but the square-root in $t = \sqrt{2y/g}$ reduces the factor to 2, not 4 or 16.
